::: {.callout-important}
All code on this page is example code — adapt to your own study variables before running.
:::

This page explains how to use [`scripts/manage_dataset.R`](https://github.com/saras-clin/UKB_help/blob/main/scripts/manage_dataset.R)
to combine extracted datasets into a single analysis-ready file.

---

## What the data looks like after extraction

After running the extraction scripts you have three separate data frames:

| Data frame | Format | One row = |
|---|---|---|
| `dataset` | Wide | One participant |
| `diagnosis_events` | **Long** | One diagnostic event |
| `prescriptions` | **Long** | One prescription record |

The diagnosis and prescription data frames are long — a participant with five
AF records across GP and HES appears five times in `diagnosis_events`. The
`source` column on each row tells you whether the event came from GP or HES.

Always run `dplyr::glimpse()` on each data frame before merging, and again
after. Joins change row counts and can silently coerce column types.

---

## GP data availability

Only about 45% of UKB participants have linked GP records. Participants
without GP linkage have **no GP events** in the extraction output — not
because they had no diagnoses, but because their records were never linked.

If your analysis uses GP data, restrict to GP-linked participants before
analysis. Including non-linked participants treats "no GP records" as "no
disease", which introduces systematic bias.

Use UKB Field **p42040** (count of linked GP clinical event records) to
identify GP-linked participants:

```r
dataset_gp <- dataset %>%
  dplyr::filter(p42040 > 0)
```

Extract p42040, p42039, and p42038 in `setup.R` step 4 if not already done.
See the [Dataset Reference](dataset-reference.qmd#sec-demographics) for details.

---

## Two approaches: all events vs. first event

| | Approach A | Approach B |
|---|---|---|
| **Source** | `extract_diagnoses.R` output | `ukbrapR::get_df()` |
| **Format** | Long — one row per event | Wide — one row per participant |
| **What you get** | Every matching event with date and source | Pre-computed first dates + binary flags per condition |
| **Use when** | Time-to-event, event counting, need all dates | Need to know if/when first diagnosed; multimorbidity; prevalent/incident classification |

**Approach A** — derive first date yourself from the long format:

```r
first_diagnosis <- diagnosis_events %>%
  dplyr::group_by(eid, condition) %>%
  dplyr::slice_min(date, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE) %>%
  dplyr::ungroup()
```

**Approach B** — `get_df()` returns a wide data frame with one row per
participant. For each condition it creates:

- `{condition}_gp_df` — first GP date
- `{condition}_hes_df` — first HES date
- `{condition}_df` — derived earliest date (GP, HES, cancer registry, death)
- `{condition}_bin` — 1 if ever diagnosed, 0 if not
- `{condition}_bin_pre` — 1 if diagnosed before baseline

```r
diagnosis_list <- ukbrapR::get_diagnoses(codes_df_combined)
diagnosis_df   <- ukbrapR::get_df(diagnosis_list, group_by = "condition")
```

After `get_df()`, replace UKB placeholder dates in GP columns with NA —
see `manage_dataset.R` Step 6 for the pattern.

Note that GP first dates (`_gp_df`) and HES first dates (`_hes_df`) can
differ for the same participant and condition. This is expected — a condition
may be recorded earlier in primary care than in hospital records, or vice versa.
The derived `_df` column takes the earliest date across all sources.

---

## Merging datasets

Join by `eid`. Always coerce `eid` to integer in every table first — a type
mismatch silently produces zero rows with no error:

```r
dataset         <- dataset         %>% dplyr::mutate(eid = as.integer(eid))
first_diagnosis <- first_diagnosis %>% dplyr::mutate(eid = as.integer(eid))
prescriptions   <- prescriptions   %>% dplyr::mutate(eid = as.integer(eid))

analysis_dataset <- dataset %>%
  dplyr::left_join(first_diagnosis, by = "eid") %>%
  dplyr::left_join(prescriptions,   by = "eid")
```

See `manage_dataset.R` Step 7 for `left_join`, `inner_join`, and count + join
options depending on your study design.

---

## Renaming and recoding

After merging, column names are still p-coded (`p31`, `p53_i0`, etc.). Rename
before analysis. See `_ignore/manage_dataset.R` for `rename_variables()` and
`recode_variables()` templates covering sex, ethnicity, smoking, physical
activity, and age at baseline.

Always run `glimpse()` on the **merged** dataset after renaming — not just on
the inputs. Joining can silently change column types.

---

## UKB built-in ICD-10 first occurrence

UKB provides pre-computed first-occurrence ICD-10 fields from HES:

- **Field 41270** — all ICD-10 diagnoses (all episodes, repeated)
- **Field 41280** — date of each diagnosis in Field 41270 (index-matched — yes, there is a date)
- **Field 41202** — first occurrence ICD-10, main position only
- **Field 41204** — first occurrence ICD-10, secondary position

Look these up on the [UK Biobank Data Showcase](https://biobank.ndph.ox.ac.uk/showcase/).

**Key limitation: HES records only.** For conditions commonly diagnosed in
primary care (hypertension, depression, most chronic conditions), Field 41270
alone substantially undercounts cases compared to combining GP and HES sources.
